description: Industry ranking per "Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture": hierarchical category scores (1–5), overall 0–100, evidence coverage reported, three lenses kept separate. DERIVED — regenerate with node tools/build-industry-ranking.mjs.

framework.category_score: Σ(parameter weight × parameter score) ÷ Σ(weights of supported parameters)
framework.overall_score: Σ(category weight × category score ÷ 5) × 100, renormalised over supported categories

scale.1: Very unattractive — materially adverse, structurally weak or unsupported by evidence
scale.2: Below average — weak outlook or economics; meaningful disadvantages
scale.3: Mixed / average — balanced evidence, average economics or material uncertainty
scale.4: Attractive — strong evidence of favourable economics or improving prospects
scale.5: Highly attractive — exceptional, durable advantage supported by robust evidence

parameters.risk_formula_note: Risk-adjusted = structural x (resilience / 5). The risk category is scored on the attractiveness scale, so 5 means MOST resilient / LEAST risk — a higher input raises the adjusted score, which is the correct direction.

value_capture._doc: Component/node value-capture weights, from the Registry Review & Recommendations §4. A separate score from the industry-attractiveness weights above — it answers 'which part of this chain keeps the money'.

industries.title: India Aircraft MRO & Civil Aerospace Components
India Battery Energy Storage (BESS)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Developer economics are set by auction, not by product: capacity tariffs fell 86% between 2022 and the ₹1.48 lakh/MW/month record of Dec-2025, and the Sep-2026 MSEDCL award at ₹2.38 lakh/MW/month sits 8.7% above its own Feb-2025 pilot only because cell prices rebounded - a 15-year annuity priced against a volatile input.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The market is ~USD 1.5 bn in 2025 rising to ~USD 7.5 bn by 2030 at ~33% nominal CAGR, against a CEA requirement of 208 GWh by 2030, ~10-14 GWh installed and a 92 GWh contracted pipeline - a pool growing at a third a year on a policy mandate rather than on demand optimism.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Awarded capacity fragments across dozens of sub-scale bidders - MSEDCL's 4 GWh went to eleven winners, the largest at 900 MW - and there is no listed pure-play, so competition is a tariff auction among project developers rather than a contest of capability.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The cycle is mid-correction: tendering fell ~66% month-on-month in Sep-2026 as authorities re-tendered 57% of capacity to chase lower tariffs, while cells (~90% imported) repriced upward and CRISIL flagged 8-9 GWh of delay risk against tariffs struck on older costs.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - the listed exposure is developer and EPC equity with no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Cells are 40-55% of system cost and ~90% imported, BMS is ~90% imported and PCS is imported; what stays in India is container and pack assembly, EMS software and thermal management - real, but a minority of the value, and the 20% domestic-content rule is met largely on indigenised software.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Grid-scale storage is a VGF-supported capital-heavy annuity: VGF Tranche II caps support at ₹18 lakh/MWh, contracts run 15 years with 95% availability obligations, and the balance sheet must carry a 12-15 year payback on an imported cost base.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Cell chemistry, BMS algorithms and PCS topologies are all bought in; what India is building is integration and control software, and the grid-forming PCS plus 10% co-location mandate from Jul-2027 raises the technical bar rather than lowering it.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Exposure concentrates in four gates: ~90% cell import dependence on China, a UL 1973 Ed.3 gate on imported BMS, re-tendering risk where L1 tariffs fall outside benchmarks, and a 2027 grid-forming mandate few domestic PCS makers can meet today.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (Alora Advisory: ~USD 1.5 bn in 2025 to ~USD 7.5 bn by 2030, ~33% nominal CAGR; Grand View’s narrower non-utility scope is shown alongside and is not averaged). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series exists.

industries.title: India EHV / HV Power Cables

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Cable makers are earning record margins on a richer EHV and export mix, with branded distribution supporting pricing power in LV/MV.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: HV cable (above 33 kV, land) Rs 8,038 cr (CY2024) to Rs 20,344 cr (CY2030F) at 16.7% nominal CAGR — the fastest voltage band — inside a wires-and-cables market going from Rs 1,00,000 cr (FY26) to Rs 1,57,500 cr (FY30).

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Consolidating into six or seven listed majors, but LV and MV remain crowded and price-competitive.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Capacity is being added into a rising market — Polycab's EHV line by end-CY2026, KEI Sanand Phase-II by Mar-2027 — with HV/EHV output up 10.3% in FY26.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Conductor drawing and insulation are domestic; HV/EHV XLPE and semiconductive compounds are foreign, and ~50% of EHV consumption is still imported.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: VCV/CCV lines are capital-heavy with 2-3 year lead times and no Indian equipment OEM — a genuine barrier that also slows capacity response.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: 550 kV is the domestic frontier and submarine cable is absent entirely — no plant and no repair ship.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Concentrated compound supply (Borouge/Borealis, Hanwha), imported EHV competition, and copper and aluminium price volatility.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Opportunity uses the same Ken Research HV series already carried in this page's Market & growth digest block. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE.

industries.title: India Green Hydrogen & Electrolyser Manufacturing

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Green hydrogen is still 2-3x grey on delivered cost, so project economics rest on subsidy, the ISTS waiver and offtake contracts rather than on the technology; stack makers and BoP suppliers earn thin, competitive conversion margins.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Green-hydrogen market USD 1.95 bn (2025) to USD 9.75 bn (2030) at 38.0% CAGR on IMARC endpoints, with 862,000 t/yr of demand and 3,000 MW/yr of electrolyser capacity awarded against ~8,000 t/yr and ~2 GW commissioned.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Stack manufacturing is crowded — L&T, Reliance, Adani, Waaree, Advait, BHEL — but almost every one licenses stack IP from Nel, McPhy, thyssenkrupp nucera or HydrogenPro, so rivalry is on balance sheet and land, not on technology.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Earliest-stage of the three energy transitions on this registry: awards are far ahead of delivery, SIGHT Tranche-I plants slipped into 2027, and no plant was fully commissioned as of Jul-2026.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series, and the pure-play stack makers are unlisted or foreign-listed.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Balance of plant is 68-76% of electrolyser cost and already ~45% domestic, which is real Indian value capture; membranes, catalysts, PTL, bipolar plates, critical minerals and stack IP all leak offshore.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Electrolyser and project capex is heavy and front-loaded against revenue that arrives after commissioning, and viability depends on a 25-year waiver and SIGHT subsidy — a financing structure, not a market one.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Pressurised alkaline is mature and PEM is scaling, with SOEC and AEM at pilot; India can assemble and integrate both but does not own the membrane, catalyst or stack design.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Demand creation is unresolved and named as the key bottleneck by SIGHT itself; iridium (~7.5 t/yr globally) and platinum are structural constraints with no Indian reserves; and SIGHT execution has slipped once already.

industries.notes: This run REPLACES the prior Market & growth block, which rested on a tier-3 source and reported 3-year and last-year splits as UNAVAILABLE. Opportunity now uses the IMARC series (USD 1.95 bn 2025 to USD 9.75 bn 2030, 38.0% CAGR) and the conflicting NITI Aayog / third-house estimates are shown as a range rather than averaged. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series.

industries.title: India Guns

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: DPSUs hold 76% of output on cost-plus deemed contracts with modest margins, while private entrants earn better returns but face multi-year qualification; ammunition value growth of ~4.93% a year caps the upside.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The ammunition pool of ₹7,057 cr in 2023 growing to ₹11,981 cr by 2032 (4.93% CAGR) sits inside a defence production base growing 15.6% a year, with propellant capacity 5–6× short of demand — real but not fast-growing substitution.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Concentrated by regulation: 788 industrial licences across 462 companies, DPSUs at 76% of production and a handful of credible private players (Bharat Forge, L&T, Adani, Solar, Reliance) — barriers protect incumbents but the single buyer holds all pricing power.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is at a record: ₹1.82 lakh cr of contracts concluded in FY26, exports +62.7%, private production at an all-time-high 24% share and ATAGS moving into delivery.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Barrels, brass cases, energetics and assembly are substantially domestic and 91% of ammunition variants are indigenised, but propellants and primers, antimony, and barrel-forging and CNC machinery remain imported.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital-intensive filling, forging and proof facilities with long qualification and heavy working capital; DPSU advances soften it, private entrants carry it on their own balance sheets.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: DRDO design capability plus Bharat Forge, L&T and Reliance tooling is genuinely indigenous at platform level, but propellant chemistry and much of the production machinery are still bought in.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: A single buyer (MoD) sets price and timing, propellant and primer supply is a wartime single point of failure, and the licensing and export-control regime constrains both entry and exit.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (KPMG ammunition market of Rs 7,057 cr in 2023 rising to Rs 11,981 cr by 2032 at 4.93%, inside FY26 defence production of Rs 1.78 lakh cr). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation data.

industries.title: India Harmonic & RV Reducers

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: There is no domestic industry to have economics: ~100% of robotics-grade units are imported, and the price a new entrant would face is set by Chinese units landing at roughly half the Japanese cost.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 10,500 robot installations in 2025 growing ~15% a year (27% CAGR over 2020–2025), with reducers at 30–40% of robot cost and 85–90% of component value imported — a real pool, but India is ~1/34th of China’s installation volume, so plant scale is hard to reach.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A global oligopoly of Harmonic Drive Systems and Nabtesco (~75% of robot reducers) over an empty domestic field: for an incumbent the moat is exceptional, for an entrant the barrier is the same wall viewed from the other side.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Robot installations are rising 15% a year on PLI-driven electronics and auto capex, but the IFR flags a possible 2026 contraction when PLI-linked investment runs out, and demand is concentrated in one buyer group.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry, and no listed Indian pure-play exists on which to build a multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India has essentially zero presence in the node, and the layers that would make it possible — gear grinding machines, CMMs, flexspline-grade steel — are themselves imported, so there is no domestic chain to position in.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capex is moderate but the real cost is time: sub-micron grinding, atmosphere-controlled heat treatment and 12–24 month qualification, with no revenue until a customer re-qualifies a joint.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The 2020 patent expiry on harmonic drives genuinely lowered the legal barrier and Chinese suppliers proved the design can be copied, but the flexspline metallurgy and grinding process remain a decade-long transfer.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Chinese price competition at half the landed cost, rare-earth and export-control exposure on precision gearing, long qualification cycles and the absence of a domestic demand anchor.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (IFR installations of 9,120 units in 2024 and ~10,500 in 2025, 27% average annual growth 2020–2025, with imports at 85–90% of component value). No rupee market size exists at Level 1 or 2, so none is stated. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE.

industries.title: India HVDC & Power Electronics

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Attractive at project level for the few qualified bidders, but converter-station content is ~100% imported, so Indian participants capture civil works and erection rather than equipment margin.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 32.3 GW NEP pipeline implying ~Rs 1.3 L cr of system capex [CALCULATED], with the market series at USD 15.07 bn (2025) to USD 31.06 bn (2035) at 7.5% — large, but the two market series conflict.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Valves and control code are a three-player global oligopoly; Indian participation is via JV and localisation mandate rather than independent capability.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Awards are lumpy and infrequent rather than cyclical — Barmer in Aug-2026, Khavda poles in 2028-29 — so order timing, not the cycle, drives sentiment.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Converter stations, DC XLPE compound and pre-moulded joints are all foreign; the localisation ladder (30% to FY28, 60% by FY35) is the only route in, and the first Indian converter-transformer order only landed in Dec-2025.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Project capital is enormous (Rs 24,819 cr for one 6 GW link) but borne by TBCB developers on regulated returns; equipment-level capex is modest.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: High-power thyristors, IGBT/SiC devices, converter control software and DC cable compound are all offshore — the deepest technology gap in the grid.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: The highest single-source concentration in the grid, plus Chinese component import relief running to Jul-2028 that undercuts the localisation case.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Opportunity uses the same HVDC series as the Market & growth digest block, with the conflicting second series disclosed rather than averaged. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE.

industries.title: India Launch Vehicles & Propulsion

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Value is genuinely migrating from ISRO to industry through ToT and consortium contracts, but launch is a low-cadence, thin-margin business today with a single anchor customer and lumpy, tender-driven revenue.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The launch segment runs from US$720 mn in 2022 to a US$3.5 bn potential by 2033 (~15.4% CAGR) inside a US$44 bn space economy, with a cadence gap of ~12 missions flown against 50–60 needed.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Very few qualified launch-vehicle primes exist anywhere, and domestically only HAL, L&T and two private entrants (Skyroot, Agnikul) — certification and flight heritage make the barrier structural rather than commercial.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Tempo and awards are at a high — SSLV ToT, the PSLV consortium, and the first private orbital launch in Jul-2026 — but the underlying mission count is still ~12 a year and demand remains programme-driven.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry, and no listed pure-play exists for private launch on which to build a multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: At ~90–95% domestic content this is the most indigenous node in the space chain — structures, motor casings, engines, avionics and materials are all sourced in-country, with only high-end electronics and some cryogenic hardware narrow-source.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Development cycles run years before first revenue, test and launch infrastructure is capital-heavy and government-provided, and demand is anchored by one customer — affordable only for large balance sheets or state backing.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Cryogenic and semi-cryogenic propulsion is a capability held by only a handful of nations, and India designs and builds its own stages, engines and avionics; SCE-200 semi-cryo extends it rather than importing it.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Single anchor customer (ISRO/NSIL), execution risk on cadence, unproven commercial scale-up at the private launchers, and long qualification — offset by near-total domestic content and policy commitment.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (IN-SPACe launch segment of US$720 mn in 2022 rising to a US$3.5 bn potential by 2033, ~15.4% CAGR). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation data.

industries.title: India Li-ion Cell Manufacturing

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A 5 GWh plant runs at roughly −10% EBITDA with breakeven near 10 GWh, and domestic cells cost 25–40% more than imports — the economics today are policy-made and sub-scale, not structural.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Cell demand of 28 GWh in 2025 rising to ~272 GWh by FY2030 (36.5% CAGR) against ~2 GWh of installed domestic capacity — the widest substitution gap of any node in the registry.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Dozens of PLI-ACC awardees and pack integrators compete at sub-scale against Chinese incumbents one to two orders of magnitude larger; domestic players are price-takers on equipment, materials and cells.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Capacity is landing into a demand pool that grows faster than it, and the ~260 GWh tender pipeline gives forward visibility — but current utilisation is close to nil and imported cells still set the price.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Cell making is the target node, but cathode and anode material, separator, copper foil and 55–60% of plant cost in machinery are all import-dominated; India’s live value-add remains module, pack and container assembly.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Cell-line equipment is 55–60% of a 5 GWh plant’s cost, EBITDA is negative below ~10 GWh and PLI disbursements begin only from FY28 — among the most capital-hungry nodes analysed.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: LFP chemistry and process recipes are licensed or bought and the equipment is overwhelmingly Chinese; India holds no proprietary cell IP and the 10-Nov-2026 machinery-control cliff sits outside its control.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: China’s export controls on LFP technology, graphite anode and cell machinery (suspension expiring 10-Nov-2026), sub-scale unit economics and a policy-dependent demand floor.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (IESA demand of 28 GWh in 2025 rising to ~272 GWh by FY2030 at a 36.5% CAGR, against ~2 GWh installed capacity). The two value forecasts disagree (17.65% vs 22.0% CAGR) and are shown as conflicting data rather than reconciled. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE.

industries.title: India Precision Machine Tools & Metrology

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Domestic builders address only about two-fifths of their own home market, with imports at ~59% of FY26 consumption, but the pool is growing ~15% a year with order bookings up ~20% — decent throughput economics behind a persistent technology gap.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Consumption of ₹36,419 cr in FY26 against ₹21,628 cr of imports is a ~₹21,600 cr substitution pool, on a 13.7% eleven-year production CAGR, with Q1 FY27 running +26% production and +20% consumption.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A fragmented domestic field (Jyoti CNC plus unlisted BFW and Ace) competes against a controller oligopoly (Fanuc, Siemens, Mitsubishi) and German/Japanese gear-grinding and metrology incumbents; rivalry is price-led in standard machines and closed in the precision tier.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The industry is in a clear upcycle: FY26 consumption +15%, order bookings +20%, and Q1 FY27 production +26% YoY, with 29 capital-goods projects sanctioned to Mar-2026 feeding forward demand.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India machines and assembles the frame, but CNC controllers, spindles, precision bearings, linear guides, ball screws and CMMs — the value-dense layers — are imported, so localisation has stopped one layer short of the moat.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Moderate capex relative to semiconductors or cells, but castings, grinding capacity and a long working-capital cycle mean entry needs patient capital rather than large cheques.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: No domestic CNC controller platform and no robotics-grade ultra-precision gear grinding or metrology; five-axis and hybrid machines are bought in, so the capability is assembly and integration rather than proprietary machine design.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Controller single-sourcing, ~30% of imports from China, exposure to US tariffs on machine-tool exports and a capex-cyclical demand base — mitigated by a large protected domestic pool and a live capital-goods scheme.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (IMTMA FY26 consumption of Rs 36,419 cr, imports of Rs 21,628 cr, and the 13.7% eleven-year production CAGR). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE because the registry carries no industry valuation data.

industries.title: India Missiles

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Integrator economics are thin and volatile: BDL’s FY26 EBITDA margin fell to 9.1%, its lowest on record, as revenue dropped 27% on a higher share of bought-out components, while electronics-side BEL earned a 30% EBITDA margin in FY26 — value sits in electronics and energetics, not in airframe integration.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The missile pool grows 39.9% a year on the narrow procurement estimate (US$468.6 mn in 2025 to US$2,512.7 mn in 2030) or 6.7% on the wider precision-guided-munitions estimate (US$2,350.6 mn in 2022 to US$3,958.6 mn in 2030); either way it sits inside FY26 defence production of Rs 1.78 lakh crore growing 15.6%, with BDL’s order book at 10.6x revenue giving unusually visible forward demand.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Design IP stays with DRDO and integration is a BDL/BEL duopoly, with private entry now opening through the Aug-2026 ToT; barriers are high and durable, but the single buyer (MoD) sets price and timing, so incumbency protects volume rather than margin.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is at a record and inflecting: FY26 defence production +15.6%, exports +62.7% to Rs 38,424 crore, BDL’s order book at Rs 26,176 crore, and FY27 guided back to ~Rs 4,500 crore revenue as delayed Akash and Astra deliveries clear.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series is carried in the registry; company multiples are reported (BDL at 70.5x FY27E EPS on Motilal Oswal’s estimates) but one company cannot define an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Around 65% of defence equipment is now produced domestically and ~91% of ammunition variants are indigenised, but seekers (Astra Mk-1), radars and specialty metals (nickel, cobalt, molybdenum, tungsten, ~Rs 8,000 crore imported) remain the imported nodes, and solid propellant is a near-duopoly.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital-heavy and slow: BDL is committing Rs 5 bn to a 160-acre naval systems plant plus the Ibrahimpatnam and Jhansi facilities, on receivables that took 109 days even after a 38% improvement; DPSU advances soften it, private entrants carry it alone.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: DRDO design capability is real and deep, but the GaN AESA seeker is still in development, scramjet/hypersonic propulsion is aspirational, and much of the precision manufacturing equipment is bought in.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: A single buyer sets price and schedule, the seeker and radar supply chain has already proven a delivery single point of failure, and the licensing and export-control regime constrains both entry and exit.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (MarketsandMarkets India missile market US$468.6 mn 2025 to US$2,512.7 mn 2030 at 39.9%, and Grand View India PGM US$2,350.6 mn 2022 to US$3,958.6 mn 2030 at 6.7%, both inside FY26 defence production of Rs 1.78 lakh crore). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation series.

industries.title: India Mobile Handsets & Accessories

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Final assembly is high-volume and thin-margin - Dixon's mobile and EMS business ran ~₹44,257 cr of revenue at ~3.5% operating margin - and the PLI-LSEM benefit ended 31-Mar-2026, removing 50-70 bps of support just as memory costs rose.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth

industries.title: India Rare-Earth Magnets

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The economics are hostile at entry: Chinese price cuts took unit import value down ~44% in one year (value +5% on tonnage +87%), and finished magnets are ~43% costlier to make in India than to import, so a domestic plant starts behind on cost before it starts.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Magnet imports were Rs 1,744 crore in FY25 on 53,748 tonnes with government projecting consumption doubling by 2030 from 2025 (~15% volume CAGR), against a Rs 7,280 crore scheme targeting 6,000 MTPA from a near-zero integrated base and import dependence of 59.6–81.3% by value — a large substitution runway, on a small rupee base.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Today the market is a 93%-China import monopoly with IREL the sole domestic oxide supplier; the scheme deliberately creates a five-player domestic structure capped at 1,200 MTPA each, so concentration is being designed in rather than competed away.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is inflecting on EV, wind and robotics volumes, but the price cycle is against producers — China resumed magnet shipments to India in October 2025 under a no-re-export condition, capping the scarcity premium.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for the magnet layer in the registry, and there is no listed domestic pure-play to derive one from.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: There is no integrated domestic plant until roughly Q1-2028; NdPr oxide supply is concentrated in IREL, heavy rare earths (Dy/Tb) for high-temperature grades are imported, and the strip caster, jet mill, vacuum sintering furnace and grain-boundary diffusion equipment are all imported — almost every link is missing.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A Rs 750 crore capital subsidy against 6,000 MTPA implies heavy capex per tonne, with a two-year gestation before first sale and a five-year incentive window that must be earned back against a falling price.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Strip-casting, jet-milling to powder, field pressing, vacuum sintering and heavy-rare-earth grain-boundary diffusion are not established in India; the government states plainly that India lacks the technology and infrastructure for the oxide-to-metal-to-alloy-to-magnet steps.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: China’s April-2025 export controls already stopped Indian production lines with two to three weeks of stock, price undercutting is documented, the beneficiary award is still pending, and the whole case rests on one scheme that has not yet delivered a tonne.

risk.name: Risk & resilience

The largest absolute profit pool in the chain, but it is not the bottleneck and four global OEMs compete on price, so margins are good rather than exceptional.

industries.title: India Satellite Payloads

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Payload economics are good where the work is design-led: Paras earned a 44% EBIT margin on its optics segment in FY26, Data Patterns a 40.1% EBITDA margin on Rs 925 cr, Centum 18-20%+ in build-to-specification against 9-10% in EMS, and Astra's management states space margins exceed defence margins. The drag is not margin but concentration: one buyer, lumpy programmes, and working-capital cycles that took Astra 374 days of cash conversion.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The demand signal is unusually explicit: 196 transponders against a stated requirement of 500 with 300 more directed, a 12-satellite EO constellation under contract to 2029, NVS-04 and NVS-05 targeted by Sep-2027, and a space economy projected from US$9 bn to US$40-45 bn. Historical growth has been slow (~1.6% a year on the economy measure), so the opportunity is forward and programme-driven rather than a trend already in the revenue line.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Design authority sits with ISRO's SAC and flight qualification gates entry, so the qualified supplier set is small and sticky - Astra has run cumulative ISRO space orders above Rs 750 cr across two decades. Barriers protect incumbency but not pricing, because the customer is the state and it sets both price and schedule.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The cycle is inflecting upward on identifiable events rather than sentiment: NVS-03 launched 30-Oct-2026 and restored the four-satellite constellation, the Rs 2,563 cr GSAT-7C whole-bus order went to NSIL in Oct-2026, the EO-PPP concession was signed in Jan-2026, and NSIL repriced Ku capacity 20% from 1-Apr-2026, the first revision in a decade.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for Indian satellite payloads, and no aggregation of listed payload-exposed companies would be a valid proxy because the exposure sits inside diversified defence-electronics businesses. Company multiples are reported (Astra at 71.7x FY26 earnings on ICICI Securities' estimates) but one company cannot define an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Domestic capture is solid at the build and screening layer and has improved twice in two years - TWTA productionisation at BEL under the SAC MoU and an indigenous clock now flying on NVS-03 - but detectors, focal planes, high-grade optics and rad-hard die remain imported, and no listed company covers the navigation payload.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Payload work is materially lighter in capital than the bus: cleanrooms, bonding and RF test benches rather than vacuum chambers and shakers, and Astra funds capex of Rs 40-50 cr a year. The burden is working capital - 374 days of cash conversion at Astra, 225-350 days on Centum's build-to-specification projects.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Design capability is real and current: SAC has delivered transponders from UHF to Ka, GSAT-N2 carries 32 beams and ~48 Gbps of Ka-band throughput, GaN SSPAs substitute for TWTAs on strategic payloads, and an indigenous rubidium clock has flown. The gap is at the component level - detector and rad-hard die design and fabrication are not domestic.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: A single state buyer sets price and schedule, four of the highest-value inputs are import-dependent under export-control regimes, qualification is gated by scarce test capacity, and payload failure is mission-ending - but the domestic trend is genuinely improving on TWTA and timing.

missing_critical: volume series (payload units / transponders over time)

value_capture.basis: Highest score on the chain: the function is essential to every transponder and SAR transmitter, was historically single-sourced abroad, and now has two domestic paths (BEL's TWTA facility under the SAC MoU, Sep-2024; SAC's GaN SSPA). Barriers are the vacuum-electronics and GaN process know-how, not capital. Rank moved up this run because BEL productionisation converts an import dependency into a domestic order book.

No substitute exists for a working clock, so pricing power and switching costs are as high as anything in the chain; the pool is small in revenue terms because there are few satellites, and it is captured by SAC rather than by any listed company. The indigenous clock flying on NVS-03 (30-Oct-2026) is the first evidence that the design can be industrialised.

The richest domestic pool by margin - Paras earned 44% EBIT on its optics segment in FY26 - with the fastest-growing demand pool behind it (12-satellite EO-PPP constellation by 2029). Scored below TWTA only because the highest-value element, the detector/FPA, is still imported and therefore not yet capturable in India.

The largest operating-profit pool available to listed investors: Astra, Centum, Data Patterns, BEL and Paras all sit here, at margins above their corporate averages. Held back by a single state buyer that sets price, and by cash conversion of 374 days at Astra.

Steady, material revenue for Astra and BEL, but the least strategic node: several qualified suppliers, no export-control choke point, and apertures below the deployable-reflector class are genuinely competitive.

Lowest score despite the highest strategic weight: the pool is currently foreign, capture in India is design-only (Aelius MMIC IP inside Astra), and a fab route would be capital-heavy with long payback. Scored as the opportunity it would become, not the pool that exists.

industries.title: Silver Paste & Metallisation

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Formulation IP and qualification lock-in give the paste makers real pricing power, and the cost base is a pass-through metal price; the economics are strong — but they accrue to Chinese-owned producers, not to any Indian entity.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India silver-paste imports US$184.33 mn in FY26, up 64.51% YoY from an implied US$112.05 mn in FY25, tracking cell capacity toward ~103 GW by Dec-2026 — fast growth on a small pool whose per-watt silver intensity is being thinned by substitution.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: An effective duopoly-plus: China is 90-92% of global PV paste output and the top three Chinese-owned producers hold close to 70%, but customers are price-sensitive and subsidy-distorted, and Chinese paste is optimised for Chinese cell lines.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Per-unit demand is in a substitution down-cycle even as Indian cell volumes rise: PV silver demand fell 6% in 2025 and is forecast down 19% in 2026, and spot silver at ~$61/oz is roughly half its Jan-2026 record, so revenue is volume-led and price-deflating.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series, and the leading paste makers are not NSE/BSE listed.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures only the upstream metal (Hindustan Zinc, Vedanta); powder, frit, vehicle, formulation, screens and printers are all imported, so domestic value addition at this node is close to zero.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality

technology.name: Technology & innovation

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: DGFT silver-bar restrictions and a 15% duty, 90-92% Chinese concentration, a technology roadmap explicitly designed to remove the product, and no domestic supplier to fall back on.

capital.basis: Moderate to heavy — shed height, crane capacity and HV test bays gate entry, and a new entrant needs two to three years to become bid-eligible.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Design IP sits abroad in IEDs, vacuum interrupters and HVDC valves; the SF6-free GIS mandate is a forced migration rather than an earned capability.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: CRGO anti-dumping outcome, the global EHV bushing shortage, Chinese OEM re-entry, and certified winding and test-bay manpower.

industries.title: India Telecom Towers

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Tower economics are a rent-plus-energy annuity with improving operating leverage: CRISIL projects Ebitdar margins at ~50% by FY28 from ~48%, RoCE rising to ~17% from ~14% and net debt to Ebitdar falling to 1.8-1.9x - among the best structural returns in Indian infrastructure.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Volume grows from 0.86 mn towers in FY26 to 1.04-1.09 mn by FY31 at 4-5% CAGR, with tenancy growth of 5-6% over FY27-28 and ₹2.0-2.1 tn of passive spend cumulatively - dependable and long, but a mid-single-digit growth pool rather than a step-change one.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The independent layer is a two-player oligopoly - Indus and Altius hold most tenanted towers - with real barriers in land, right of way and site power, but the customer side is three telcos, so the oligopoly faces a monopsony.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Tenancy growth has recovered to 5-6% after moderating to ~4% in FY26, yet revenue per tower is falling ~2.0% YoY against 5.9% co-location growth - volume improving while price erodes.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: Indus trades at ~6.4x/6.0x FY27E/FY28E EV/EBITDA, a discount to global tower peers in sell-side work of Jul-2026 [REPORTED-T3]; cheap for an annuity, but the series covers only one listed proxy.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Towers, shelters, foundations and erection are domestic and the rent stays home; what leaks is narrow but real - LFP cells, rectifier semiconductors and small-cell/DAS silicon.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Roughly ₹10,000 cr of annual capex across FY27-28, funded mainly from internal accruals with leverage at 1.8-1.9x - capital-heavy but self-funding, with the maintenance tail (lithium retrofit, solarisation) a standing call on cash.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The asset is mature passive infrastructure; the new capability gates - DCIP active sharing from Jul-2026, solarisation and lithium retrofit - are integration and energy-management problems rather than new technology.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three dated cliffs sit inside two years: the Jio tenancy renewal in H2 FY27 (up to 15% of Indus revenue, with sell-side modelling ~5,000 exits), Vi funding (over 30% of revenue), and continuing ARPT erosion.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (0.86 mn towers FY26 to 1.04–1.09 mn FY31 at 4–5% CAGR, REPORTED-T2, with the CALCULATED 3.9–4.9% shown alongside). Valuation is scored from one listed proxy’s EV/EBITDA, labelled [REPORTED-T3], not from an industry series.

industries.title: India Vehicles & Auto Components

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A ~17% five-year CAGR on a large base, but the industry is structurally a converter of steel, aluminium and imported electronics - value leaks to cells, semiconductors and magnets, and supplier margins sit under OEM bargaining power.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Turnover ₹7.60 lakh crore in FY2025-26 at ~17% five-year CAGR [REPORTED-T2: ACMA, Jul-2026], with import substitution in cells, electronics and magnets as the identifiable growth pool.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Highly fragmented across 1,000+ firms with strong OEM countervailing power; consolidation and PLI scale requirements are slowly raising concentration.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Mid-cycle: FY26 grew 12.7% but H1 FY26 decelerated to 6.8%, and ACMA guides 8-10% for FY27 with a GST cut supporting the second half.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Bottlenecks are named and quantified - rare-earth magnets 60-80% of value imported, Li-ion cells and automotive semiconductors largely imported - each a defined substitution pool.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Working capital is the real burden (receivables from OEMs plus inventory), while fixed capex per node is moderate and PLI-Auto subsidises part of it.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Predominantly build-to-print; R&D and IP are thin, and the EV transition shifts content toward technologies - cells, power electronics, ADAS - that are imported.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Diversified across vehicle segments, exports and a large aftermarket, which cushions cyclicality; magnet supply and tariff exposure are the live vulnerabilities.

value_capture.basis: Content per vehicle keeps rising and qualification cycles are long, so pricing holds; the pool is small in Indian hands because almost all of it is imported.

The largest and fastest-growing pool in the chain and the binding bottleneck - and the worst cash-conversion business in it: gigafactory capital, ramp losses and returns that only appear at high utilisation.
The largest absolute profit pool in the ecosystem and the reason component suppliers earn little: OEM countervailing power is exactly what compresses the tier below.
High barriers and the fastest content growth, but almost entirely imported today, so the Indian chain captures integration rather than the profit pool.
Cash-generative and mature with an installed base that keeps it running, but the pool is in structural decline as EV content displaces engine and driveline value.
The commodity middle: real capacity and real barriers to entry, but pass-through pricing, weak switching costs and returns set by the metal cycle.
Assembly-level work below the cell, growing fast but squeezed between cell suppliers upstream and OEMs downstream, with thin value-add per pack.
